overview: The Shan states were a changing network of principalities, not one kingdom. Valley towns and upland communities had different rulers and relationships with neighbouring courts. The imported outline includes Guwahati in Assam but omits Kengtung; regional examples below extend beyond its shading. This 1530 to 1783 record cannot reliably show individual boundaries or independence. Its dates are map coverage, not the birth and disappearance of Shan people.

periods.title: Shan power and Burmese expansion
periods.summary: The regional balance changed as Bayinnaung captured Ava and several major Shan centres.

periods.title: Local courts and wider networks
periods.summary: Cross-border commerce developed alongside local political relationships.

periods.title: Early Konbaung period
periods.summary: Shan principalities operated within overlapping regional relationships.

items.text: Northern Tay or Shan forces took Ava in 1527, shortly before this map begins. Historian Ken Kirigaya connects that victory with competition for a valuable river trading centre. Rubies, jade, amber and musk linked the inland region to southern ports and wider markets. These principalities could shape lowland politics as well as respond to it.

A large surviving bell at Shwezigon in Bagan preserves Bayinnaung’s own account of expansion. Its Burmese, Mon and Pali texts record the capture of Ava in 1555 and campaigns against Mong Mit, Hsipaw, Mohnyin and Mogaung in 1557. The bell is a contemporary royal claim, to be read with the conqueror’s viewpoint in mind.

Conquest could leave a local royal house in place. U Thaw Kaung’s study describes Bayinnaung reinstating defeated rulers after they swore allegiance and retaining ministers. Rebellion could instead bring removal. A town might therefore keep its court while its ruler owed service to a stronger king.

From the seventeenth century, frontier commerce benefited from rulers who maintained recognition at both Chinese and Burmese courts. Jingli Bai’s study follows tea and cotton moving outward, and metals and spices arriving through caravans and rivers. Its Sipsong Panna case illustrates the wider Tai commercial world, rather than proving that every place shaded here belonged to one government.

In the Konbaung period, these polities included both valley farmers growing wet rice and upland communities cultivating cleared plots in shifting cycles. Feeding a town involved different landscapes and kinds of work. Calling the whole region simply a land of mountain farmers misses the productive valleys between the hills.

sections.title: Reading the evidence on stone and paper

items.text: Two British Library rubbings turned out to preserve different pieces of the same stone. In 2025, epigrapher Nuttapong Punjaburi matched its fragmented faces. The original 1537 inscription, in Tai Khoen and Fak Kham script, records instructions for lay followers at Wat Pa Mai. Fak Kham means tamarind pod, a deliciously memorable name for curved letters.

A text added to that stone in 1600 records a donation to Wat Phiang Sri of 400 rice fields with people or farmers, plus a Buddha image valued at three baht. The wording places agricultural labour alongside temple wealth. The people supplying food were part of the institution’s economy, although this fragment cannot tell us their individual family arrangements.

The poet and monk Sao Dhammadinna, traditionally dated 1541 to 1640, helped make Buddhist teaching accessible in Shan verse. His Sutta Nibbāna means Discourse on Nibbāna. In an introduction he admired his teacher at Wan Khang monastery. That personal acknowledgement gives us a glimpse of a learning relationship behind the finished text.

Dhammadinna’s work continued to be copied for families remembering the dead. A manuscript now at the Rylands Library preserves a message that donating a book earns merit but does not replace living well. Its completion note gives 6 January without a year, so the surviving copy cannot be assigned to the poet’s lifetime.

That Rylands volume also explains why books need not look like books on our shelves. Its extremely thin paper has writing on only one side; the leaves are folded double, sewn along the top and stored rolled up. Such suspended books are called pap kin. The paper is probably bamboo paper, rather than securely identified by laboratory testing.

A dated later writing sample is ဗုဒ္ဓါနူဿတိ, transliterated Buddhānūssati, meaning recollection of the Buddha. This Pali title labels a Shan Buddhist manuscript, British Library Or 12040, dated 1885. The Burmese-script characters follow the curator’s transcription, rather than reproducing the handwriting. The text concerns mindful recollection of the Buddha’s qualities.

Later Shan folding books could resemble gold bars when closed. Craftspeople lacquered and gilded their covers, sometimes adding raised decoration and coloured mirror glass. Or 14572, dated 1894, weighs more than two kilograms. Not exactly a pocket book!

These household observations are later than the map. In her 1910 book, Leslie Milne describes mothers packing rice and curry separately in banana leaves for children tending cattle, tying the parcels with bamboo strips. Some children had only rice. A leaf could do the job of a lunch box, but this account also records uneven access to food.

Milne also described preparing bamboo for houses: stems were soaked for days or weeks, and builders chose an auspicious day to begin. Her account estimates sixty or seventy large bamboos and at least a hundred smaller ones for a small house. This is a colonial-era observation of building work and belief, not a standard blueprint for every earlier Shan home.

Surviving Shan manuscript collections include texts about healing, charms and tattooing alongside Buddhist teaching, history and stories. SOAS researchers are cataloguing this varied knowledge. The collection does not by itself establish which remedies were used in a particular sixteenth-century village, and these texts are evidence of practices and beliefs rather than proof that a treatment worked.

A Penn Museum report published in 1961 describes Hopong’s market recurring every fifth day. Pa-oh neighbours brought produce from surrounding hills, including garlic and strawberries in May, and bought manufactured goods. This later scene shows different communities sharing a regional economy after princely powers changed. It is not evidence that the same produce filled a market stall in 1530.

ending.text: Nothing in the evidence identifies 1783 as a collective fall of the Shan states. Principalities continued under changing overlords and later colonial rule. By the 1961 Hopong account, the government had purchased most sawbwas’ old powers, while a ruling family still occupied its residence. Political institutions changed; Shan communities and their neighbours continued.
